title: the Rudram
hook: the hymn leaves the page and goes into the temple, where it is chanted while water pours over the stone
tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum

segments.voice: Yesterday the Rudram turned around and asked: cha me, and to me, right down to grain and a shared meal. Your line was the Rudram. Who did you eat with? Today is our last day inside the hymn. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

A small brass pot hangs on a chain above a stone linga. There's a pinhole in its base, and water drips, one drop and then the next, onto the top of the stone. In some Shiva temples that slow drip is kept going through the day. On festival days it grows into something louder. Priests sit close around the linga, and while water and milk are poured over it, they chant. One of the hymns they may chant is the one we've been living in: the Rudram. It was never only something to read. It's something to pour to. So today, on our last day with it, we follow the hymn out of the book and into the bath.
screen: `A POT, A PINHOLE, A STONE.` → `PRIESTS CHANT AS THE WATER POURS.` → `OUT OF THE BOOK, INTO THE BATH.`

segments.voice: The bath is called abhisheka, and when the Rudram is chanted with it, people call the whole rite Rudrabhisheka. Hold the hymn up next to the water and its shape starts to show. Remember how it opens. It bows to Rudra's anger, to his arrow, to his bow and his arms, and it asks that the arrow be turned away and the bow unstrung. It begins with a fierce god and an honest fear of him. Then it keeps bowing, and as it bows it finds Rudra everywhere: in the forest and the field, among carpenters and chariot-makers, even, startlingly, as the lord of thieves. Nothing is left outside the bow. Deep inside the hymn comes the line namah shivaya cha shivataraya cha: salutation to the kind one, and to the one kinder still. There's a traditional saying about this. The Rudram sits at the heart of the Vedas, the five syllables namah shivaya sit at the heart of the Rudram, and the two syllables shi-va sit at the heart of those five. Take it as a picture, not a measurement. The movement is real either way: from a god with a drawn bow, inward, toward a name that means auspicious, gentle, kind. And the water is making the same movement. Another old saying puts it in a few words: Vishnu loves to be adorned, Shiva loves to be bathed. The one with fire in his third eye and poison held in his throat is offered coolness, again and again. So the hymn and the pouring do one job together. They turn toward the frightening edge of things and meet it with a bow, one drop at a time, until it shows a kind face.
screen: `ABHISHEKA: THE SACRED BATH.` · `IT OPENS WITH RUDRA'S ANGER.` · `SHIVA SITS AT ITS HEART.` · `SHIVA LOVES TO BE BATHED.` · then, large: `TO THE KIND ONE, AND KINDER STILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a slow pour. Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Bring to mind one thing that feels fierce right now: a worry, a person, a deadline with its bow drawn. Don't fight it, and don't fix it. On each out-breath, picture cool water poured slowly over it, the way water pours over the stone. One breath, one pour. Let the thing stay what it is. Just keep pouring. If you pray, you can say namah shivaya softly with each pour, or the name of God you use. The bell holds the time.
The Rudram. A Vedic hymn that bows to the fierce Rudra again and again, until Shiva, the kind one, appears at its heart. Today, chanted while the water pours.
Your line: the Rudram. Today, when something fierce comes at you, give it one slow breath before you answer, like water over stone. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In Shiva temples and in homes, Hindus may chant the Rudram during abhisheka, pouring water, milk and other offerings over the linga; some families arrange a Rudrabhisheka for a festival, a new home, or a hard time.

original.note: Sanskrit: Rudra, the Vedic name the hymn bows to, the fierce form of Shiva.

notes: Last of the Rudram days (1146–1152). Review picks up 1151 (the chamakam, cha me). 1146–1151 covered the opening to Rudra's anger, the sun, namah, the short and tall, trees and foam, and the chamakam; this day takes the hymn into abhisheka and the namah shivaya line, recalling the opening only briefly.

Confirm: the dripping vessel (dhara patra) over the linga in some Shiva temples; 'Rudrabhisheka' as the name of the rite; the opening of the namakam (namaste rudra manyava...) paraphrased as bowing to anger, arrow, bow and arms and asking that the arrow be turned away.

Confirm the namakam's salutations to the lord of thieves (stenanam pataye / taskaranam pataye) and to carpenters and chariot-makers (takshabhyo rathakarebhyash cha), and the gloss of shivataraya as 'kinder still / more auspicious'.
The 'heart of the Vedas' saying (Rudram > Panchakshara > shi-va) is presented as a traditional saying and 'a picture, not a measurement'; confirm wording and that it is not mis-attributed.
'Alankara priyo vishnuh, abhisheka priyah shivah' paraphrased as an old saying; confirm.
Practice invites saying 'namah shivaya' with each breath, an existing mantra, not a new prayer.
